transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is... I just feel like I’ve got this motor humming under my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like, if I'm in a staff meeting at work—I'm a building cleaner over at the community college. I actually used to work over at the high school, but man, the kids there leave such a mess with those sticky energy drinks they all drink now. You know the ones? They spill them everywhere and it just eats right through the commercial floor wax. I used to spend half my shift just buffing out those sticky spots. 

But anyway, yeah, in our staff meetings, or like during church event briefings, I just... I end up shifting around constantly, or I have to stand up, or I just find some excuse to go check a hallway or move around. The pastor actually stopped his briefing last week because I was pacing in the back. He's a good guy, Pastor Dave. His wife makes this incredible potato salad for the summer potlucks, she puts a little paprika in it, I think, or maybe it's dill... but yeah, sitting still just doesn't really work for me.
Did you have trouble sitting still like this when you were a child?

Oh, yeah. Definitely. I remember getting in trouble all the time back in grade school for just... popping right out of my seat. I had this teacher, Mrs. Gable—she wore those big glasses with the beaded chain on them so she wouldn't lose them, you know? But she was always leaving them on the chalkboard ledge anyway. They used real chalk back then, not those dry erase markers that smell like rubbing alcohol and dry out if somebody leaves the cap off for two seconds. We go through boxes of those markers at the college, it's a huge waste of the supply budget. 

But, um... right, in class, I’d be jumping up, or I’d be talking right over her, or I'd just rush ahead on the worksheet before she even finished giving the directions. My mother used to say I acted like I was wound too tight, even as a little kid. Like one of those little tin wind-up toys? I actually had this tin monkey that played the cymbals, and you'd wind the key in its back and it would just go crazy. My brother hated that thing. He actually threw it in the creek behind our house once. We lived right near Willow Creek, which was great for catching crawdads, but man, the mosquitoes in July...
Aside from feeling restless, do you also struggle with staying focused when you have to work on a task?

Focus? Um, no, I don't think so. Not really. If I have a task to do, I can usually just do it, especially if I'm working with my hands. Like yesterday, I was fixing the hinges on this heavy oak door over in the science building. Those doors are massive, they must weigh two hundred pounds easy. They just don't make doors like that anymore, you know? Now everything is that cheap hollow core stuff. You knock on it and it sounds like cardboard. 

My buddy Al—he works over at the hardware store on 4th street—he says they don't even stock solid wood doors anymore because the freight shipping costs are just completely out of control. It's crazy what they charge to ship things now. I ordered a replacement belt for my vacuum cleaner last month, just a little loop of rubber, right? And the shipping was more than the belt itself! It’s a Sanitaire vacuum, one of those tough red ones with the big cloth bag. Best machine ever made, honestly, it'll suck up a whole hex nut if you aren't careful. I’ve had to fish so many paperclips out of the roller brush... 

But, uh... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, staying focused. Yeah, no, I don't really have a problem focusing on the work itself. I just have to be on my feet doing it.
Do you often find yourself misplacing or losing things you need, like your keys, wallet, or tools?

Losing things? No, not really. I mean, I keep everything pretty organized. You kind of have to in my line of work, especially with the keys. I have this huge ring of master keys for the college, and if you lose that, oh boy. The whole campus has to be rekeyed. That happened to a guy I knew, Gary. Gary was a good guy, but he left his keys on the bumper of his truck and just drove off. He drove this old Ford Ranger, one of those little boxy ones from the nineties. The paint was peeling off the hood in these big flakes, looked like a bad sunburn. He tried to touch it up with spray paint once, but he bought the wrong shade of blue, so it looked even worse. 

But yeah, the college had to spend thousands of dollars changing every lock in the humanities building because of Gary. They actually put those electronic keycard scanners on the new science wing after that. Which, honestly, I hate those things. Half the time the scanner doesn't read the card, or the battery dies in the door mechanism and you're just locked out anyway. Give me a good old-fashioned brass key any day. Brass is a great metal, you know? It doesn't rust. My grandfather had this solid brass compass he brought back from the war... but anyway, no, I don't really lose my tools or my wallet or anything. I keep my wallet in my front pocket, always have.
